task.title: Inspect due schedules against an explicit cutoff
task.objective: Complete issue https://github.com/Knosence9/project-vela/issues/819 by exposing pending due work without ambient clock or mutation authority.
acceptance_criteria: Add vela-dev schedule due with one exact non-negative Unix-millisecond cutoff.
Use the typed read-only list_due projection and preserve due-instant then exact-ID ordering.
Include only pending schedules due at or before the inclusive caller-supplied cutoff.
Emit no partial output and never create storage, claim, dispatch, materialize, or execute work.

attempts.diagnostic: The focused integration test failed because due was an unrecognized schedule subcommand.
attempts.patch: Added inclusive cutoff, deterministic ordering, lifecycle filtering, empty result, invalid cutoff, and missing-database non-creation tests.

attempts.diagnostic: The kernel due projection was unavailable to operators and reading ambient time would make inspection nondeterministic and broaden authority.
attempts.patch: Parsed an exact u64 cutoff before storage access, called ScheduleStore::list_due, and reused the existing compact schedule projection and complete serialization path.

attempts.summary: Waited for genuine hosted review coverage.
attempts.diagnostic: CodeRabbit first returned a rate-limited false green and later remained pending after the Rust quality gate succeeded.
attempts.patch: Kept auto-merge unarmed until the substantive four-file review completed with no actionable comments and confirmed explicit-time, no-mutation behavior.

outcome.summary: Callers can deterministically inspect pending schedules due by an explicit instant without granting the CLI clock or lifecycle authority.

verification.command: nix develop --command cargo test --locked -p vela-dev --test cli schedule

lessons: Accept time as explicit caller evidence when a read-only query does not need ambient clock authority.
Parse bounded input before opening storage so invalid requests cannot trigger filesystem side effects.
Reuse kernel ordering and filtering instead of recreating scheduler semantics in the CLI.
Due inspection identifies candidates; it does not reserve, claim, dispatch, or execute them.
